title: I watched Gone Girl for the firs time.. And I don't see why it's so highly rated.

commenti.body: [removed]

The only thing I liked about that movie was the very bleak commentary on the institution of modern marriage; the conclusion there is that they deserve each other in their horrible fake selves that is all for show and vague self-validation. No connection, no compassion—very contemporary message.
[removed]

one of the reasons why Gone Girl is such a divisive film is because it is a film that challenges the viewers to question their own assumptions, expectations, and perspectives. It is a film that shifts its tone, genre, and point of view several times, and it does not provide easy answers or clear moral judgments. It is a film that invites multiple interpretations and reactions, and it does not shy away from exploring the dark and disturbing aspects of human nature.

Couldn't have said it better myself. The twists and turns are gripping but it's the ending that is the most twisted thing of all, no matter how you interpret it. I expected nothing going in and it ended up my favourite film of its year.

>I actually feel rather insulted in how women are supposed to relate to that personality (which clearly the film is trying to make you do).

Is it though? I mean, I'm a guy so I wouldn't really know but I don't think I've seen any women/girls in their right mind who've said they find Amy relatable at all. They recognise that she's a sociopathic b-word.

Sure the 'Cool Girl' monologue (Which plenty of people quote, including me) is intended for us audience to understand why Amy was forced to do what she did, but she's isn't painted as a hero whatsoever. Both Nick and Amy are terrible people in a symbiotic cycle of doom that destroy everything around them unless they play each other's game. Us audience are just voyeurs sneaking in their lives to watch it unfold. Like Fincher says, 'People are perverts'.

That's just my take.
I think for normies it is even more shocking

Potentially controversial ramble incoming!
I liked exactly what you disliked.

I can totally understand the discomfort, for instance, in Amy staging a sexual assault, because in reality that's extremely rare and not how I want women to be represented or how I want any woman to act. 
But Amy doesn't have to represent "women", she can just be crazy Amy.

And yet... In how many films do male characters do horrific things, yet still manage to be anti-heroes? "Morally grey"? "Complex"? Their rage is often justified. Revenge movies are popular. 

There's something deeply seductive for me about enjoying Amy's nutso behaviour. The men she hurts with it are *awful*.
I've rarely seen anything like it in film. Amy channels the (overstated) fear of crazy, lying bitches, and takes it to level 100. It's so wrong it's right. And yet, because we want to be better in reality, we clutch our pearls and say "omg why are we being represented like this? I can't root for her!"

But lots of people root for Tyler Durden. Or Patrick Bateman. Or The Joker. Because, in the words of Quentin Tarantino, "violence is fun!"

So basically, yeah, I don't want to race men to the bottom IRL. This doesn't reflect my actual moral compass. But god damn was it a guilty pleasure in this film.
I couldn't get past the first scene (the two main characters meeting). The dialogue was so pompous and cringe I couldn't take it. I had a gutteral "no no no" and reached for the remote.

Amy has some relatable attributes, like all good characters, but no, the stuff she does isn't supposed to be typical or representative. When she does her crime, the story isn't saying, "This is the sort of thing lots of women do." So, it really doesn't make sense criticize the story on the basis that lots of women don't do that.

But that's just it.. She isn't really being forced to do what she does, that's I think the problem with it. The monologue and many similar things she expresses are meant to be relatable to women, and I certainly have seen a lot of people admire that mindset.

Of course not all women will find her a character to empathise with but plenty seem to, I personally find it a very shallow portrayel of experienced misogyny.

Gillian Flynn said that she wanted to make a story about a female villain. Female villains can have layers … they may even have a compelling “reason” for it, but they use it to commit atrocities. That’s what makes it so fun.

You definitely have a point in that many male characters are shown to be bad people yet still admired in certain aspects.. I suppose my gripe with it is more that it feels contrived and superficial.

I will say that I found 'The Handmaiden' to be much better motivated in it's 'revenge against men' plot and less shallow.

It's totally fine that you didn't like it like. It's not necessarily a must watch for me. It was a great first watch for me personally trying to figure out wtf is going on. I'll pop the blu-ray in just because i enjoy the sibling relationship.

Hmm, not sure I can fully agree with that, I don't find it offers all that much to speculate about.. Though for me personally the most challenging thing about it is that it is such a crude showing of a woman with horrible morals. Although the husband is obviously not likable I'd say he was actually a more nuanced character as a whole despite not being the protagonist of the story.

I would agree that it's a rather cynical take on marriage, obviously though that is what happens when 2 self-important people get into a relationship expecting to live their perfect idea of a marriage.. Wouldn't say it's a contemporary message necessarily but certainly bleak.

Of course it's not an exposition on realistic behavior from women.. My opinion is just that she isn't really a good character, I actually found her lacking in depth and consisting of a lot of tropes, I guess it made it hard for me to find her believable as a character.

>Perhaps  I'm a little bit of a film snob but I feel there are many films out  there that explore a lot of these things in much more interesting ways  and go more in depth.

Like what?

But what are the layers? What is the motive?

It seems to simply be that she's a narcissist, all her reasons come back to her wanting to be acknowledged and admired. I don't know what layers I'm missing here.

I agree with the lack of nuance and some of the things Amy pulled were far fetched. But i've never heard anyone really find Amy as a character relatable. Some of the things she felt and experienced were, but her actions were psychotic. I think, also, there is the satisfying thing that a husband got his. He is a cheating, superficial, uncaring slob, married to a more capable woman, who, as we learned in the beginning, sacrificed a lot for him. So the ending is satisfying, in a way. Two terrible people stuck with each other in their misery. Also performances are great. Cool girl monologue lives rent free, lol.

Films that explore troublesome marriages, narcissism, manipulative behaviors, misogyny, the exploitation of the media during times of tragedy.. All of these themes are explored in so many other films. I feel like Gone Girl tried to touch on all of these things but I just didn't find it particularly gripping in this film.

What in particular would you like a title example of?
The sibling relationship was probably the high point of the film I will say.
Lol, Nick’s cheating with a much younger woman wasn’t a motive to you?
Sure… I’m asking you to list some examples since you said you know of so many better ones.

The incessant manipulation makes it contemporary—the very subversal of trust in all respects, interpersonal and institutional. The totalitarian aspect of it, so to speak. Now that I’m thinking about it, I’ve begun to like the movie more, so thanks for that.

Perhaps the word 'relatable' wasn't the right term, English isn't my first language but I can't think of what would be a better word to use.

I would like to challenge the idea that she is a more 'capable woman' since she was raised in wealth and privilege (in many ways), her intelligence obviously is one thing in which she is a capable person but she didn't seem to have any real goals for herself and lacking empathy to the degree she shows is also something to inevitably become a problem. On paper she seems like a more well-adjusted person, but she clearly isn't, plus her positive personality traits seem to only exist to fuel her narcissism, to show some sort of superiority.

And we do mostly see him through the lens of an unreliable narrator so it's hard to take anything on face value in that sense.. It's satisfying to see a bad person get what they deserve but I didn't feel that so much here since it wasn't entirely clear how much of his character was just her lies and perspective (like him being violent, we don't know if he really was violent), manipulative people also often use withholding affection and sex as a way to get their partner to trip up for example. For that reason I didn't find that to be particularly satisfying.

I honestly don't have much to complain about in regards to the acting, definitely some good performances.

No, because she doesn't care that he doesn't love her, she just feels like he considers her inferior to a younger woman (that she looks down on) when it comes to sexual attraction.

That's still narcissism.
Yes but across several layers it’s primarily a movie about (heterosexual) relationships and/or marriage and most people consider infidelity a pretty serious betrayal

>Side-note: The only other female revenge movies I can think of are 'The Handmaiden' and 'Sympathy For Lady Vengeance'. And those have much worse reasons for the act of vengeance.

Have you seen A Promising Young Woman? I feel like it qualifies for this category

\-Troublesome marriages: Closer (2004), American Beauty, The Piano, Who's afraid of Virginia Woolf.. etc

\-Narcissism/Manipulation: Mommy Dearest, Fear (1996), Gaslight, Cracks.. etc

Now the theme of misogyny I'd say is very much up for interpretation but it's obviously a topic that comes up in many films.

These are just a couple I could think of, I could share a bunch with female psychopathic characters as well but I'll leave it at this for now.

When did Amy say or suggest she didn’t care that Nick doesn’t love her? 

I haven’t watched the movie in several years, but I can remember her being extremely hurt when she witnessed him cheating and recycling a cherished “sugar storm” memory of theirs with his mistress. I got the impression that seeing that made her feel like their whole origin story had been a lie.

It also isn’t “narcissistic” to want to be admired and/or acknowledged by your *spouse*. Nick was quite neglectful towards her after their move. I think the movie made an interesting point about the betrayal one can feel when you actually get to know your partner intimately (ie, not just the “idealized” version we all put forward when dating).
I haven't! I need to though. Did you feel that it did a good job of revenge?

>I haven't! I need to though. Did you feel that it did a good job of revenge?

It was a good exploration of the subject, and a film that I enjoyed. Don't expect Kill Bill, though. That's all I'll say!

Same thing here.

For me this movie is only half as clever as it thinks it is...

Great casting though, I think Fincher did a great direction but it did not resonate with me on an emotional level.

"Sharp objects" with Amy Adams by the same author hits way deeper. It's a great mini-series !

The motive is that she pretended to be the perfect woman to a mediocre man and he still wanted more. Amy had always struggled with feelings of inadequacy due to her parents writing children's books with a character who had her name but was more accomplished. Then Nick took her away from New York and her entire world, moved her to a small town where she has no friends, no stimulation, and then cheats on her with one of his students, which adds even more insult to injury in Amy's mind because it's so cliché. To Amy, being the boring, neglected suburban housewife who gets cheated on is too much to bear. The point is that a lot of women can relate to this but none of them do what Amy does because they aren't insane. She took it to an extreme and does something real women only fantasize about when they find out they've been cheated on by the men they've sacrificed everything for.

I don't really see many tropes, there aren't a whole lot of films like this, but there are a plethora of films on the other side with psychotic, narcissistic, insane men. So it's refreshing to see it from the other side.  I don't really find people like Tyler Durden to be believable, or Patrick Bateman, but that doesn't mean they arent well thought out, structured, complex characters, and Amy is no different. A character doesn't need to be realistic to be complex or have depth.

You also have to understand that this book and especially the movie jump-started this whole unreliable narrator, mastermind woman thing for this generation. There is a LOT of content now directly pulled from this movie so it may feel heavy-handed to you because you have been experiencing the products of it for several years. 
But it’s always interesting to see how people respond to Amy as opposed to (as someone points out above) Patrick Bateman, Tyler Durden, Walter White, etc. I  fact I’d say almost all male protagonists are unlikeable because we assume they’re not the default.

Folks, OP is not deserving of the downvotes. Their post and comments are detailed, respectful and are a good faith individual assessment of the film. We need to resist the urge to downvote when we disagree, even when we think they aren’t “getting it”.

that’s what makes her a monster, that she wasn’t forced to do anything, she’s a bad person all on her own. Pressure from her parents books create self-image issues for her to be angry at, but end of the day, she’s a psycho, no matter how you slice it.

Also Revenge (2017)

It's explicitly putting the woman into a male role, evoking a Schwarzenegger-esque action hero as she relentlessly hunts down her attackers

Well I can name a few.. high strung wife, femme fatale (literally in the name), the intelligent and cold psychopath, 'not like other girls' that almost crosses into manic pixie dream girl (but doesn't because it's only to show a part of her narrative).

Of course a character doesn't need to be realistic or complex or have depth, but I prefer that for a protagonist in a film that is so heavily relying on personality.

It's not really a nitpick if I have issues with the main elements of the movie to be honest, that's why it's a hot take apparently.

The acting is definitely good, I definitely won't claim otherwise, perhaps I just find Fincher to be too on the nose in his approach.

I think you are being downvoted mostly because of your title where you question the legitimacy of everyone else’s ratings of the film. It’s kind of annoying when people do that. Plus, your main complaint seems is that the portrayal of Amy is somehow “dangerous.” I personally find it sad when audiences won’t allow women characters to be just as terrible as men characters in movies because they are supposed to somehow represent all women. You let this belief get in the way of enjoying a really fun, twisty ride.
Nonetheless it has been said better than I could've...
